title: Security review - encryption/KMS/BYOK/HSM - Orchid Health
summary: Orchid Health ran a security review focused on encryption controls for Redwood Inference. Main asks: BYOK with HSM-backed keys, separation of control plane and data plane keys for private/dedicated deployments, key rotation/rotation windows, audit logs for key usage, and attestation/FIPS compliance. Redwood clarified envelope encryption, customer-managed keys options (AWS/GCP/Azure & external HSM), private deployment integration points, and next steps to share SOC2/ISO artifacts and a detailed KMS architecture doc and pilot plan.
next_steps: Redwood to send SOC 2/ISO reports and KMS architecture doc (Maya) by 2026-11-03
Schedule follow-up deep dive on BYOK integration with Orchid infra (Alex/Lina) week of 11/8
Run a short POC for envelope encryption performance impact with 1 model route (Priya)

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-10-30
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Alex (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE), Sam (Orchid Head Security), Lina (Orchid Cloud Infra), Tom (CTO), Jamal (Compliance)

Summary/Context (auto): Orchid is evaluating Redwood for inference of PHI-adjacent data. Primary blockers are key management and evidence for encryption controls. They prefer BYOK with HSM-backed keys and need clear separation of control/data plane.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, then we'll jump into encryption and KMS. Alex, do you wanna kick off on the high level?
[00:18] Alex Rivera: Yeah, sure. Hi, I'm Alex, solutions eng on the infra side. Today we'll cover how Redwood handles at-rest and in-transit encryption, our KMS integrations, BYOK workflows, and options for HSM-backed keys. We'll also touch on audit logs and attestation.
[00:35] Sam Patel: Great, thanks. Our constraints are basically: we need customer-control of keys for anything with PHI-ish data, strong auditability, and FIPS-compatible HSMs ideally. Also separation we want the control plane not to have unwrap privileges for customer keys.
[00:52] Alex Rivera: Totally. At a high level, Redwood supports envelope encryption by default; we encrypt data with a per-tenant data key, and that data key is wrapped by a master key in KMS. For Hosted customers we offer Redwood-managed KMS or integrate with cloud KMS (AWS/GCP/Azure). For Dedicated/Private we support BYOK where you hold the key material in your KMS or HSM.
[01:20] Lina Gomez: When you say "wrap" \u2014 does the Redwood control plane ever hold the unwrapped data key in plaintext?
[01:27] Alex Rivera: We try to minimize exposure. In the hosted default, wrapping/unwrapping occurs in a secure key service we manage; ephemeral plaintext keys are kept in memory in a hardened enclave and are never persisted. For BYOK with Private, the unwrap operation can be done by a customer-controlled key service in their VPC or on-prem HSM\u2014 so Redwood's control plane wouldn't have the plaintext.
[01:52] Tom Reed: So for our case we'd want the unwrap to happen inside our VPC, using our KMS/HSM, right?
[01:58] Maya Chen: Correct. That's the BYOK pattern. You point Redwood at your customer-managed key endpoint\u2014whether AWS KMS with an import or CloudHSM-backed CMK, or an external HSM accessible over secure network\u2014and Redwood will perform envelope encryption where only the wrapped data leaves your boundary.
[02:18] Jamal Brooks: We need to validate attestation \u2014 like FIPS 140-2/3 level and module IDs. Do you have a list of supported HSM vendors and FIPS statements?
[02:28] Alex Rivera: Yes. We commonly work with AWS CloudHSM, AWS KMS (with Dedicated HSM backing), Thales Luna, and YubiHSM for smaller use cases. We can provide the FIPS certs and module ids. For hosted customers we also publish the FIPS posture of our providers. We'll include that in the doc.
[02:46] Sam Patel: Also, key rotation policy \u2014 we have requirements about rotation windows and cryptoperiods. If we rotate the CMK, how does that impact existing wrapped data keys and cached KV caches?
[02:57] Alex Rivera: Good question. Our envelope approach means existing data keys remain valid until we rewrap. Rotation typically involves generating a new CMK and re-wrapping the DEKs (data encryption keys) lazily\u2014we rewrap on first write or on a background job. For cached KV entries we support a TTL; when a rewrap happens, subsequent decrypt attempts will use the new CMK or trigger rewrap. We can coordinate a forced rewrap if you need an immediate rewrap window.
[03:25] Lina Gomez: You mentioned KV cache \u2014 I sometimes see notes in your docs about "KV cache" and "kayvee cache" in older exports, just making sure that's not something proprietary.
[03:34] Priya Singh: Yeah, apologies \u2014 Fireflies sometimes transcribes "KV" as "kayvee". It's just key-value cache in the inference runtime (KV for attention cache), not related to KMS keys.
[03:44] Sam Patel: Makes sense. For auditability we need granular logs showing keystroke \u2014 I mean key usage \u2014 like decrypt requests, which principal requested unwrap, and the full chain of custody. Do you expose those logs to customers?
[03:59] Alex Rivera: For Dedicated and Private, yes. We push detailed key usage logs to the same logging destination you configure \u2014 CloudWatch/Stackdriver/Azure Monitor or your SIEM via syslog. Logs include timestamp, operation (Encrypt/Decrypt/Sign), key id, request id, and caller principal. For hosted customers with Redwood-managed KMS we provide an audit feed and periodic reports, but not direct raw stream by default \u2014 we can arrange export for the enterprise plan.
[04:25] Tom Reed: What about separation of privileges? We can't have Redwood engineers unilaterally able to unwrap keys.
[04:31] Maya Chen: Understood. For Private/BYOK the unwrap capability is gated by your key policies. Redwood only authenticates using a service principal in your account/tenant. If you restrict IAM policies to require custom approvals and deny our service principal the Decrypt permission, then Redwood can't unwrap. Alternatively, you can route unwrap calls through an internal proxy that enforces approvals.
[04:53] Jamal Brooks: We also want hardware attestation for the enclave that handles ephemeral keys. Do you support Nitro Enclaves or SGX-based attestation for the control plane?
[05:03] Alex Rivera: We run a mix. Our cloud providers use Nitro Enclaves for isolated key handling on EC2 where applicable, and we support SGX in some on-prem blades. We can provide attestation evidence. For Private deployments we can also run the key unwrap inside your HSM so attestation is handled by your infra.
[05:29] Sam Patel: Okay. Two more things: in-transit encryption \u2014 TLS is table stakes, but we need mTLS between control and data plane, and client cert rotation.
[05:40] Priya Singh: We support TLS1.2+/1.3 with strong ciphers and mTLS between internal services. For Dedicated/Private we can provision mutual TLS with your CA or use certs provisioned into your control plane. Client cert rotation is automated if you use Redwood-managed cert rotation; otherwise you can manage certs in your CA.
[06:00] Lina Gomez: Another operational question \u2014 where are keys stored for hosted Redwood-managed KMS? Are they in HSMs?
[06:07] Alex Rivera: Our managed KMS uses cloud provider KMS which is HSM-backed under-the-hood. The master keys are provider-managed CMKs, typically HSM-backed. We do not store raw key material on disk; CMKs are managed by the provider and comply with their FIPS statements.
[06:23] Sam Patel: On data residency \u2014 our data must remain in US East and EU West depending on region. How does key residency tie to data residency?
[06:33] Maya Chen: Keys and wrapped DEKs are colocated with the data region. For hosted we can provision CMKs in the matching cloud region; for Dedicated/Private you control region via your KMS/HSM. We can enforce routing by policy so requests for EU data use EU keys physically located in that region.
[06:51] Tom Reed: About multi-tenant isolation: if we use Dedicated GPUs but still in Redwood's control plane, how do you ensure keys aren't accessible by other tenants?
[07:01] Alex Rivera: Dedicated capacity means a single-tenant GPU pool but the control plane may be shared logically. We maintain per-tenant key namespaces and access controls; unwrap operations require the tenant's key id and are authorized per-tenant. For absolute isolation you can opt for Private deployment where the control plane sits in your VPC.
[07:20] Sam Patel: We have a preferred KMS vendor \u2014 HashiCorp Vault with an HSM (PKCS#11) interface. Can Redwood integrate with an external Vault that exposes PKCS#11 or HTTP signing endpoints?
[07:31] Alex Rivera: Yes. We support PKCS#11 and HTTP KMS endpoints. For Vault we typically use their transit secret engine where Vault holds or calls the HSM for sign/unwrap. We have sample connectors and terraform snippets we'll share.
[07:47] Lina Gomez: Any latency impact? Our inference tail latency SLOs are tight. If every token causes a KMS unwrap that's non-starter.
[07:56] Priya Singh: Right \u2014 we do not call the KMS on every token. Envelope encryption means the data key is used locally inside the runtime once unwrapped and cached. Subsequent inference ops use the cached DEK for crypto ops. Unwrap happens on initial load or when cache TTL expires. That dramatically reduces KMS calls. We can instrument and show expected QPS and cache hit rates with your workload.
[08:20] Sam Patel: Good. How about key compromise rotation or emergency key purge? If a master CMK is compromised, can we revoke access and rewrap data quickly?
[08:29] Alex Rivera: In an emergency we can coordinate a key disable/disable policy with your KMS provider. We also support emergency rewrap operations\u2014there's a process to rotate CMKs and force rewrap of DEKs. It requires coordination since large datasets may take time; we can prioritize routes that store PHI. We also maintain point-in-time backups of wrapped keys to enable rollback if necessary, subject to your policies.
[08:55] Tom Reed: For the compliance team \u2014 audit trails and attestations \u2014 can we get a live feed into our SIEM of every Decrypt/Encrypt event?
[09:03] Alex Rivera: Yes for Dedicated/Private. For hosted-managed customers we provide periodic export; for enterprise we can set up streaming into your SIEM (Kafka/Cloud Pub/Sub/syslog) with the appropriate PII redaction.
[09:22] Jamal Brooks: A nit \u2014 please ensure logs don't contain unwrapped plaintext or tokens.
[09:26] Priya Singh: Absolutely. Logs include key ids and metadata, never plaintext keys or decrypted data. We also support redaction hooks on the logging pipeline.
[09:36] Sam Patel: Are your key policies versioned and accessible? We need to audit changes to the policies that grant Redwood decryption rights.
[09:44] Alex Rivera: Yes \u2014 key policy changes are tracked in the KMS provider and we can surface a history. For integrations via Vault we can also push config diffs to your audit service.
[09:56] Lina Gomez: If we go the BYOK route, what's the onboarding effort? How long to stand up and validate integration?
[10:03] Maya Chen: Typical enterprise onboarding for BYOK + HSM is 2-6 weeks depending on approvals and network setup. We have a checklist: attestations, firewall rules, service principal setup, sample terraform, perf tests, and an audit review. We'll provide an onboarding playbook.
[10:22] Tom Reed: Ok, next I'm curious about HSM vendor lock-in \u2014 if we switch from vault+HSM to cloud KMS later, what's migration like?
[10:30] Alex Rivera: Migration usually involves creating a new CMK in the target KMS and then doing a rewrap of DEKs from the old CMK to the new CMK. We can orchestrate that with a migration job; complexity depends on data volume, but it's straightforward with our tooling.
[10:47] Sam Patel: One last technical: can we require customer-side attestation tokens for each unwrap call? Like a signed policy token?
[10:55] Alex Rivera: Yes, we support signed attestations and signed requests\u2014mutual attestation tokens that your KMS can require as part of the unwrap call. That adds an extra layer of proof prior to granting Decrypt.
[11:08] Maya Chen: Alright, let's wrap with next steps. We'll send the SOC2 and ISO artifacts, FIPS/HSM vendor list and module IDs, onboarding checklist, and some sample terraform/connectors. We'll also schedule a follow-up technical deep dive to work through Vault+HSM specifics.
[11:24] Sam Patel: Sounds good. Please include explicit details about: where the unwrapped keys live in memory, eviction policy for caches, and the exact log fields we can expect.
[11:32] Priya Singh: We'll include those. Also we'll run the envelope encryption perf microbench and share numbers by 11/5.
[11:39] Tom Reed: And legal will need the attestation and data residency commitments for the contract.
[11:44] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll attach those items. Thanks everyone.

(End of main discussion)
